v: Somewhere between a VERY GOOD movie and a GREAT one. Raw, honest and instantly relatable for anyone who was never the class topper — though that refusal to add commercial sugar may keep the regular time-pass crowd away.
e: Needi Naadi Oke Katha stays admirably raw and focused instead of adding commercial distractions. That same honesty may limit its reach with viewers looking only for easy entertainment, but average and below-average students can connect instantly with its pressures, its idea of what it means to ‘settle’ in life and Sree Vishnu’s wonderfully natural performance.
body:
Somewhere between a VERY GOOD movie and a GREAT movie!!!!!

Kudos to the director for keeping Needi Naadi Oke Katha raw, focused and completely to the point without forcing commercial ingredients into it.

Ironically, that is also what may prevent the movie from connecting with a section of the regular audience that enters a theatre mainly for time-pass entertainment.

Story-wise, though, it feels absolutely apt.

Any average or below-average student who has grown up under constant pressure about marks, jobs and the need to ‘settle’ in life can connect with the film almost instantly.

One dialogue especially stayed with me: there was a time when getting a government job meant you were settled; later it became a bank job; now it has become a software job!!!!! 🙏

That one thought captures so much of the constantly changing definition of success around us.

And Sree Vishnu… such a natural performer 🙏

After watching him here, I made a mental note not to casually miss his films.

v: Hmmm… totally disconnected!!! Pretty visuals, mature performances and a few lovely dialogues cannot rescue a love story whose love-at-first-sight logic and familiar ego clashes simply do not work for me.
e: Tholiprema may have worked for almost everyone around me, including my friends and parents, but I remained completely disconnected from its romance. I liked several dialogues, the cinematography and the mature work from Varun Tej and Raashii Khanna; unfortunately the contrived romantic setup and familiar hero-heroine ego conflict overwhelmed those positives for me.
body:
Hmmm… I felt totally disconnected!!!!!

Maybe I first need to understand why I have become so resistant to pure love stories 😄

I was actually trying to remember the last full-fledged romance I genuinely loved — Love Aaj Kal? Cocktail? Anand? Godavari?

My bigger problem is that I keep waiting for our filmmakers to give us more realistic love stories instead of repeatedly falling back on love at first sight, convenient situations and the assumption that the heroine will eventually fall for the hero because he fights for her.

Some scenes here simply pushed that irritation further.

Who gets off a train these days to fetch drinking water from a tap? 🙏

And the hero-heroine ego conflict is something Telugu cinema has been revisiting since at least Kushi.

Having said all that, almost every friend of mine liked the movie — even my parents liked it.

So perhaps the only fair explanation is: thanks, RGV, for completely messing up my taste for love stories!!!!! 😄

P.S. When the entire Telugu audience was going gaga over Ye Maaya Chesave, I was probably one of the few people who hated that too 😦

I did love a few dialogues here, especially the thoughts about caste, remembering people’s mistakes more easily than their love, and how those who pretend to be angry with us can sometimes be the ones who love us most.

The cinematography and visuals are excellent, and Varun Tej and Raashii Khanna give mature performances.

Those positives are real — the romance simply did not connect with me.

v: You may leave thinking it was AWEsomely AW(E)ful or AW(E)fully AWEsome — but every few minutes it gives you something to feel AWE about. Regina, the terrific BGM and witty, thoughtful dialogues stand out.
e: AWE! is the kind of unusual film that can divide viewers completely, yet its ambition kept surprising me throughout. Regina Cassandra delivers the standout performance, the BGM is terrific, the humour often carries a thoughtful edge and even the lone song neatly reflects the film’s central conflict.
body:
After watching AWE!, you may come out feeling it was AWEsomely AW(E)ful or AW(E)fully AWEsome 😄

But one thing is almost guaranteed: every five or ten minutes, the film gives you something that makes you feel AWE!!!!!

The BGM is terrifically AWEsome and plays a huge role in holding together such an unusual collection of moods and characters.

There are many performers in the film, but Regina Cassandra’s terrific performance definitely stands out.

The dialogues are humorous and thought-provoking, especially the exchanges involving Nani, Priyadarshi and Ravi Teja, along with a couple of lovely lines from Nithya Menen.

There is only one major song, but the lyrics are excellent.

“Shatruvai dehame… manasutho thalapade” almost sums up the entire story in a single line 🙏

Whatever side of the awesome-versus-awful debate you finally land on, this is definitely not a movie that passes without making an impression.

v: All that struggle for what felt to me like a very thin story of two married men obsessed with one woman. Ranveer, a few grand low-light frames and Bhansali’s final stretch are the limited saving graces.
e: Padmaavat left me wondering what inspired Sanjay Leela Bhansali to fight so hard to make this particular story. The film is visually grand in places and Ranveer Singh is terrific, while Ratan Singh’s death and the jauhar sequence show Bhansali at his strongest; unfortunately Shahid Kapoor and Deepika Padukone feel badly underused and the core story never held me.
body:
I kept wondering what inspired Sanjay Leela Bhansali to take up this project against so many odds.

For me, underneath all that scale and controversy was a surprisingly thin story about two already-married men and their obsession with one woman.

Apart from a few beautifully composed low-light grand frames and Ranveer Singh’s terrific performance, I found very little in the film that held me.

Shahid Kapoor has enormous acting talent, yet here he often feels reduced to a single-expression supporting presence.

And Deepika Padukone — who has delivered good performances even in films I disliked badly — is given such a restrained character that she too often feels almost expressionless.

There are moments where Bhansali’s brilliance absolutely shows.

The sequence in which Ratan Singh dies while fighting Khilji is handled powerfully.

And the entire jauhar episode is staged with the visual and emotional command you expect from Bhansali 🙏

I only wish the rest of the movie had given me enough story and character engagement to match those few standout stretches.
